title: Impacts of a concentrated solar power trough facility on birds and other wildlife in South Africa
abstract: This study assesses bird and wildlife mortality and changes in bird species communities at a 50 MW utility-scale concentrated solar power parabolic trough facility in South Africa. The facility was searched for evidence of large vertebrate mortalities over three months. Eight bird carcasses were recorded in the solar field, all of which probably died prior to the study period. Carcass persistence trials indicated that 94% of bird carcasses survived 24 h, 68% for 7 d, and 56% for 28 d, although persistence varied with carcass size. No large carcasses (>1 000 g) were removed entirely by scavengers after 28 d, whereas only 42% of medium-sized (100–1 000 g) and 17% of small (<100 g) carcasses remained after 28 d. Searchers detected 72% of bird carcasses, with large birds more likely to be detected than small birds. The extrapolated mortality rate for the facility was 3.9 birds y−1 (90% CI 0.0–14.9) or 0.1 bird fatalitites MW y−1 (90% CI 0.0–0.3). Birds were much more abundant (141.9 birds km−1) and species rich (51 species) in the surrounding rangeland than in the solar field (1.27 birds km−1; 22 species). Of the 24 bird carcasses found in the evaporation ponds, six likely drowned (four species). Three reptiles (one species) and 12 mammals (seven species), including sensitive species such as aardvark Orycteropus afer, also drowned in the evaporation ponds. This is the first study of its kind in South Africa and unexpectedly revealed that the evaporation ponds had a bigger impact on wildlife than anticipated.

## **Impacts of a concentrated solar power trough facility on birds and other wildlife in South Africa**

## **Corey Jeal[1,2] , Vonica Perold[1] *, Samantha Ralston-Paton[3] and Peter G Ryan[1]**

_1 FitzPatrick Institute of African Ornithology, DST-NRF Centre of Excellence, University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa 2 Chipembele Wildlife Education Trust, Mfuwe, Zambia_

_3 BirdLife South Africa, Johannesburg, South Africa_

_* Corresponding author, email: vperold@gmail.com_

**This study assesses bird and wildlife mortality and changes in bird species communities at a 50 MW utility-scale concentrated solar power parabolic trough facility in South Africa. The facility was searched for evidence of large vertebrate mortalities over three months. Eight bird carcasses were recorded in the solar field, all of which probably died prior to the study period. Carcass persistence trials indicated that 94% of bird carcasses survived 24 h, 68% for 7 d, and 56% for 28 d, although persistence varied with carcass size. No large carcasses (** > **1 000 g) were removed entirely by scavengers after 28 d, whereas only 42% of medium-sized (100–1 000 g) and 17% of small (** < **100 g) carcasses remained after 28 d. Searchers detected 72% of bird carcasses, with large birds more likely to be detected than small birds. The extrapolated mortality rate for the facility was 3.9 birds y**[−1] **(90% CI 0.0–14.9) or 0.1 bird fatalitites MW y**[−] **[1] (90% CI 0.0–0.3). Birds were much more abundant (141.9 birds km**[−] **[1] ) and species rich (51 species) in the surrounding rangeland than in the solar field (1.27 birds km**[−] **[1] ; 22 species). Of the 24 bird carcasses found in the evaporation ponds, six likely drowned (four species). Three reptiles (one species) and 12 mammals (seven species), including sensitive species such as aardvark** _**Orycteropus afer**_ **, also drowned in the evaporation ponds. This is the first study of its kind in South Africa and unexpectedly revealed that the evaporation ponds had a bigger impact on wildlife than anticipated.**

## **Impact d’une installation solaire par concentrateur parabolique sur les oiseaux et autres espèces sauvages en Afrique du sud**

**Cette étude a pour but d’évaluer la mortalité des oiseaux et d’autres espèces de la faune sauvage ainsi que des changements dans la communauté aviaire au sein d’une centrale solaire de type Concentrateur Solaire Parabolique d’une puissance de 50 MW en Afrique du Sud. Il a été réalisé une recherche de mortalité des larges vertébrés au sein de l’installation pendant 3 mois. Huit carcasses d’oiseaux ont été retrouvées au sein du champs des panneaux solaires, tous probablement morts avant la période de suivi effective de cette étude. Les tests de persistance des carcasses ont indiqué que 94% des carcasses persistent 24 heures, 68% sept jours et 56% 28 jours, bien que la persistance des carcasses varie selon la taille de celles-ci. Aucune grosse carcasse (< 1 000 g) n’a disparu après 28 jours alors que 42% des carcasses de taille moyenne (100–1 000 g) et 17% des petites tailles ont demeuré après 28 jours. Le taux d’efficacité des chercheurs de carcasses d’oiseaux a été de 72% avec une probabilité de détection plus forte concernant les grands oiseaux que les petits. Le taux de mortalité extrapolé était de 3,9 oiseaux par an pour l’installation (90% IC 0,0–14,9) ou 0,1 oiseau par MW installé et par an (90% IC 0,0–0,3). Le cortège d’oiseaux était beaucoup plus abondant (149 oiseaux/km) et diversifié (51 espèces) dans l’environnement proche qu’au sein de la centrale solaire (1,27 oiseau/km ; 22 espèces). Des 24 carcasses trouvées dans les bassins d’évaporation, six ont probablement trouvé la mort par noyade (4 espèces). Trois reptiles et douze mammifères (7 espèces, dont des espèces sensibles comme l’Oryctérope** _**Orycteropus afer,**_ **se sont aussi noyées dans le bassin d’évaporation. Cette étude est la première de la sorte en Afrique du Sud et elle révèle étonnement que les bassins d’évaporation ont de plus forts impacts sur la faune sauvage que prévu.**

**Keywords:** carcass persistence, collision impact, concentrated solar power, evaporation ponds, mortalities, searcher efficiency

**Online supplementary material:** Supplementary information for this article is available at https://dx.doi.org/10.2989/00306525.2019.1581295

## **Introduction**

The environmental benefits of renewable energy are well known (Haddad and Dones 1991; McCombie and Jefferson 2016), but trade-offs between the advantages and impacts on the environment while transitioning to a green economy

receive less attention (Gasparatos et al. 2017). Impacts, specifically on birds, have been widely documented at wind energy facilities (Kunz et al. 2007; Hull et al. 2013; Erickson et al. 2014; May et al. 2017), but there are few studies on

the impacts of utility-scale solar energy (USSE) facilities on birds and other vertebrates (McCrary et al. 1986; Hernandez et al. 2014; Kagan et al. 2014; Walston et al. 2016). Three main technologies are used for USSE production: (1) photovoltaic (PV) solar panels, (2) concentrated solar power (CSP) towers, and (3) CSP parabolic troughs. The CSP trough technology uses parabolic mirrors to concentrate solar radiation on a tube containing heat transfer fluid (HTF), which is relayed to a power block where either steam is produced to drive a turbine, or heat is stored to produce steam at a later stage.

The type of solar energy technology, combined with size and location of the facility, are likely to affect the nature and magnitude of impacts on birds and other vertebrates (Hernandez et al. 2014; Walston et al. 2016; Gasparatos et al. 2017). Collision with solar panels or mirrors can occur across all three technologies, whereas solar flux trauma is limited to CSP. The larger the facility, the more likely it is to have a bigger impact with regards to displacement and habitat loss of species. The location of a facility is important, as biodiversity loss can be reduced by developing on previously degraded lands or increased when developments are cut out of pristine habitats (Peschel 2010; Visser et al. 2019).

Two causes of bird mortality specific to CSP facilities have been identified: (1) collision impact and (2) solar-flux damage (McCrary et al. 1986; Kagan et al. 2014; Smith and Dwyer 2016; Walston et al. 2016). Collision mortality results when birds strike a part of the solar infrastructure, such as solar panels, mirrors, transmission lines or support structures. Collisions also can result in indirect mortality when birds are left debilitated after impact, reducing flying, foraging and predator avoidance ability, and ultimately resulting in death. Solar flux (concentrated solar radiation) mortality occurs when birds are exposed to extreme temperatures, usually around the receiver at the top of a CSP tower, where temperatures can exceed 400 °C (McCrary et al. 1986; Kagan et al. 2014; Smith and Dwyer 2016; Walston et al. 2016). The water used to cool turbines is often treated with chemicals (e.g. selenium) to prevent fouling and to control the pH (Lovich and Ennen 2011). This water is stored in evaporation ponds to allow concentration of chemicals before disposal. In addition to collision and solar flux impacts, evaporation ponds at solar power facilities have been identified as areas of potential impact as they attract animals and could be a source of selenium toxicity (Herbst 2006; Lovich and Ennen 2011), linked to high egg mortality and birth defects in birds using the ponds (Tanji et al. 2002; Marn 2003).

The first published study of bird mortalities at a USSE facility found that collision impacts were the main cause of death, accounting for 81% (57/70) of mortalities recorded over 40 weeks at Solar One, a 10 MW CSP tower facility in the Mojave Desert (California, USA), whereas only 19% (13/70) were due to burning by solar flux (McCrary et al. 1986). More recently, however, most bird deaths that could be ascribed to a specific cause at Ivanpah, a 390 MW CSP tower facility in the Mojave Desert (California, USA), resulted from solar flux (60%, _n_ = 47), even though the towers were not actively fluxing (not operational) for seven months of the 17-month study period (Kagan et al. 2014).

Only 31% ( _n_ = 24) of bird deaths were due to collision impacts, 6% ( _n_ = 5) to predation, and 1% to electrocution and starvation ( _n_ = 1 each), but the cause of death could not be determined for 45% of carcasses ( _n_ = 63 of 141 carcasses; Kagan et al. 2014). There are scant data for the impacts of CSP trough facilities. Kagan et al. (2014) reported 31 bird mortalities over an unspecified time period at Genesis, a 250 MW CSP parabolic trough facility in the USA. The cause of death was inferred for only eight birds, of which six (75%) were due to collisions and two (25%) due to predation trauma. Walston et al. (2015) reported that at Mohave Solar (a 250 MW CSP trough facility in California, USA), 14 incidental fatalities were recorded in eight months, but no causes of death were identified. In both studies, recording of mortalities was opportunistic without a systematic sampling design or correction for searcher detection or carcass persistence bias.

Assessing the direct impacts of USSE facilities and similar infrastructure on birds and other vertebrates typically depends on observers searching the facility for evidence of wildlife mortality (Ponce et al. 2010; Huso 2011; Korner-Nievergelt et al. 2011; Costantini et al. 2016). It is important for the crude mortality estimates to correct for detection biases resulting from observers failing to find all carcasses (searcher efficiency) and removal of carcasses by scavengers prior to routine mortality surveys (Smallwood 2007; Sovacool 2009; Huso 2011; Huso et al. 2016; Costantini et al. 2016). Searcher efficiency trials determine the detection probability of carcasses in relation to searcher experience, vegetation type, carcass size and species (Schutgens et al. 2014; Huso et al. 2016). Persistence trials assess the rate at which scavengers remove carcasses, which is influenced by carcass type and size (Costantini et al. 2016). Correction factors to account for carcass detection and persistence biases need to be estimated for each study site because they depend on site-specific characteristics such as vegetation cover and height (detection bias) and the local scavenger community (persistence bias).

Bird communities at USSE facilities also can be affected by landscape-level changes, such as habitat fragmentation, degradation and loss (Kagan et al. 2014; Smith and Dwyer 2016; Walston et al. 2016). USSE facilities require large spatial footprints of 1.4 to 6.2 ha per MW of production (Walston et al. 2016), and usually involve extensive removal and control of vegetation (Hernandez et al. 2014). CSP trough facilities typically have more stringent vegetation control than PV sites (Dessouky 2013) because the flammable heat transfer fluid (HTF) poses a fire risk (Grippo et al. 2014), and thus the degree of habitat transformation compared with the pre-construction state is greater. Another possible impact of solar facilities is the emission of polarised light (Walston et al. 2015). This may attract invertebrates and hence insectivorous birds, increasing the birds’ risk of collisions or damage through solar flux (Horváth et al. 2010; Walston et al. 2015). There are also concerns about the ‘lake effect’ (Kagan et al. 2014), whereby solar arrays could be mistaken for a waterbody by wetland birds, which often fly between wetlands at night. This might explain the collision of waterbirds recorded at solar facilities in the USA (Kagan et al. 2014). However,

there is little evidence for these potential impacts (Lovich and Ennen 2011; Kagan et al. 2014; Walston et al. 2015).

McCrary et al. (1986) is still the only systematic study on the impacts of a USSE CSP tower facility published in the primary literature, although there are several grey literature reports summarising impacts at other tower facilities and some trough facilities. McCrary et al. (1986) recorded 70 bird mortalities of 26 species over 40 weeks at the Solar One facility, with a scavenger removal of 10% to 30%, giving a mean mortality rate of 1.9–2.2 birds week[−1] . Walston et al. (2016) estimated an annual bird mortality rate of 3.96 birds MW[−1] over 377 MW from solar-related fatalities at the Ivanpah CSP tower in the USA (based on Harvey and Associates 2014). When combining known and unknown causes, the fatality rate per year was 9.30 birds MW[−1] . These estimates were adjusted for searcher efficiency and carcass persistence. With only one published systematic study for CSP towers and only incidental evidence for CSP parabolic trough facilities, providing no fatality estimates (Kagan et al. 2014; Walston et al. 2015), there is a strong need to investigate the impacts of this technology outside of the USA. This is essential, especially when anticipating cumulative impacts prompted by the rapid growth of the solar industry in South Africa (DoE 2015). Our study is the first to systematically assess the impact of a CSP parabolic trough facility on birds and other wildlife in Africa. Based on our findings, we provide recommendations for threat management and mitigation.

## **Materials and methods**

## _**Study site**_

This study was conducted at the ACWA Power SolAfrica Bokpoort 50 MW CSP Power Plant located in the Northern Cape, South Africa, approximately 30 km north-west of

Groblershoop on the boundary between the Nama-Karoo and Savanna biomes (Figure 1). The area is dominated by Kalahari Karroid Shrubland with elements of Gordonia Duneveld on flat, gravel plains (Mucina and Rutherford 2006). The mean annual precipitation is 100–200 mm and the site has the highest recorded solar radiation in winter for the Nama-Karoo (Mucina and Rutherford 2006). Land use in the area is predominantly stock (cattle and sheep) and game farming, with irrigated agriculture along the Orange River valley, c. 14 km south of Bokpoort. Commercial operation began in March 2016.

The facility has a footprint of 200 ha, comprising a solar field of 360 rows of parabolic mirrors (troughs), with 24 sections (each consisting of 28 mirrors, 2.89 m × 1.70 m) per row (Figure 1). Rows are c. 300 m long, giving a total solar collector length of c. 108 km. Water for the facility is pumped from the Orange River and stored in two ponds (85 m × 85 m) for use in the power block. Waste water is disposed of in two shallow evaporation ponds (200 m × 280 m) lined with black PVC membranes to prevent seepage and increase water temperature to promote evaporation. They have an operational depth of <50 cm and a maximum depth of 1.5–1.75 m. The entire facility is surrounded by a 2.5-m-high mesh fence.

## _**Carcass searches**_

The study was conducted from September to December 2016. The solar field was divided into eight subfields (40–50 rows of mirrors each; Figure 1). An observer walked adjacent to the mirrors to search for bird or other wildlife carcasses. When a carcass was found, it was photographed, identified to species, the location recorded and surrounding infrastructure searched for evidence of collision (e.g. mirror smudges or impact sites). Carcass decomposition rates, determined by environmental

conditions such as temperature and level of invertebrate activity, influences time of death estimation (Smallwood and Karas 2009). We assumed a carcass was fresh (c. <1 week) if soft flesh, fresh feathers or blood were present (Smallwood and Karas 2009). Carcasses were classified as old (>1 week) if dried flesh, weathered and discolored feathers or bleached exposed bones were present. Carcasses were removed to avoid double counts.

A comprehensive survey of the entire solar field (360 rows) was conducted in September and December 2016. In addition, every second row (180 rows) was surveyed at four-week intervals in October, November and December. An intensive 6-day survey was conducted on 35% of the solar field (125 rows) where groups of 10–11 rows were surveyed daily. The intensive surveys were evenly spaced within the facility except for a group of 30 rows in an area of high bird activity, to maximise the chance of detecting any collision mortalities. The evaporation and holding ponds were surveyed four days each week between 16:00–19:00 ( _n_ = 53 checks). Dead animals were searched for by cycling, walking or driving slowly around the edge of the evaporation ponds. When possible, carcasses were removed to avoid double counts. All carcass searches were performed by a single observer to keep sampling effort constant.

## _**Searcher efficiency trials**_

Searcher efficiency trials were conducted in September 2017, using four searchers. Each searcher took a turn to distribute 18 bird carcasses under 10 mirror rows (c. 3 km), while the remaining three searchers took turns to search for the carcasses. This gave 54 possible detections per trial, and four trials, each in a different location, and thus a total of 216 possible detections (Supplementary Appendix S1). Carcasses were divided into three size classes: nine small birds (<100 g), six medium-sized birds (100–1 000 g) and three large (>1 000 g) birds. Frozen whole carcasses were used, as unlike the wind industry, it was not expected that collisions with infrastructure would result in dismemberment (Smallwood 2013).

## _**Carcass persistence trials**_

Carcass persistence trials were conducted throughout the study period, using 34 bird carcasses: nine small (<100 g), 16 medium (100–1 000 g) and nine large (>1 000 g). Carcasses were frozen from a fresh state and, although some bird carcasses used were sourced from unlikely habitats (e.g. seabirds), potentially affecting the likelihood of scavenger removal (Ponce et al. 2010), they resembled water birds found at the site in terms of size, weight and colouration. Carcass handling time was minimised to avoid scent contamination, which could be used as cues by predators or scavengers (Whelan et al. 1994). Carcasses were distributed evenly across the solar field to eliminate effects of natural edges, human disturbance and vegetation changes over the three-month study, and were placed within the solar field in locations mimicking mirror collisions. Carcasses were checked daily for at least the first 6 d after placement, every second day until day 14, and then at days 21 and 28, when monitoring stopped. The state at each check was classified as: (1) intact (whole carcass,

undamaged except for invertebrate activity); (2) scavenged (carcass remained but some flesh or feathers removed); (3) feather spot (carcass removed but sufficient feathers remain to identify the presence of a carcass); (4) removed (no evidence of carcass). Nine carcasses were monitored with Ltl-5310 ACORN motion-triggered scouting cameras to identify scavengers. The probability of carcass daily survival was estimated using Mayfield’s (1975) at risk approach, in which the number of carcass removals is divided by at risk days to calculate daily removal probability.

## _**Fatality estimate**_

The estimated number of birds killed by collisions was extrapolated from the observed collision data, correcting for detection biases and carcass persistence. A program developed by the United States Geological Survey called Evidence of Absence software (EoA) was used to calculate mortality rates where very low numbers of carcasses have been detected (Dalthorp et al. 2017). We adapted our data (by excluding daily-checks and only incorporating full checks) to adhere to program specifications. The EoA software can be used to estimate the total mortality ( _M_ ) presenting data as the total upper bound number of fatalities (assigned to a user’s credibility level, e.g. 1 − α) that can possibly occur at the facility per year. It also estimates the mortality rate parameter (λ), which is the average fatality event rate. EoA expresses the uncertainty about λ as a posterior distribution of λ with a 90% confidence interval (CI).

## _**Bird communities**_

Bird community surveys were conducted throughout the study period in the solar field and adjacent rangelands. Surveys within the solar field were conducted in conjunction with carcass clearance checks. The mirrors restricted the lateral field of view to 50 m, so all birds seen in the 300-m-long transect lines (the length of a mirror row) were identified using binoculars and recorded. Surveys were conducted from 06:00 to 11:00 and 15:00 to 19:00, with each 300-m-long transect lasting c. 20 min. The rangeland sampling site (350 ha) was of similar topography, geology and vegetation structure to that of the facility pre-construction (van Rooyen 2010). In the rangeland, 44 transects (each 500 m in length and lasting c. 30 min) were walked between sunrise and 09:30 when it was cooler and birds were more active. All birds seen were identified to species level using binoculars, and the perpendicular distance of the bird from the transect line was estimated and recorded in four categories: <50 m, 50–100 m, 100–200 m and >200 m. However, in order to compare with the solar field counts, only birds within 50 m of the transect line were counted, and expressed as birds seen per kilometre of transect. In addition, birds at the evaporation ponds and holding ponds were surveyed in conjunction with each mortality check, identifying and counting all bird species using binoculars and/or a spotting scope.

All birds were assigned to foraging guilds to assess community differences between the solar field, adjacent rangeland and evaporation ponds (Simberloff and Dayan 1991). To compare bird abundance and species richness between the solar field and rangeland transects, zero

inflated modelling in R 3.3.2 (R Development Core Team 2016) was used to account for the excess of zero counts in the solar field counts. Transect lengths were offset in the model to account for their different lengths. The model tested the number of birds per transect as well as number of species recorded per transect.

## **Results**

## _**Carcass searches**_

Eight bird carcasses from at least four species were discovered within the solar field (Table 1), but all were estimated to have died before the three-month monitoring period. Five carcasses were discovered during the initial clearance sweep, and only one (Cape Turtle Dove _Streptopelia capicola_ ) was recent (<1 week), likely due to collision impact (Table 1). Three additional old carcasses were found during subsequent searches, after being overlooked among vegetation during the initial clearance. Western Barn Owls _Tyto alba_ made up half of the mortalities and live owls were common in the solar field (Table 1) where they roosted in the torque tubes. On occasion, owls flushed from the tubes during the day were observed swiping or colliding with mirrors with no noticeable negative impact. Of the seven carcasses that could be identified, six were medium-sized birds (100–1 000 g) and one small (<100 g; Table 1).

During the study, 37 carcasses of 15 species (seven birds, seven mammals and one reptile) were found in

the evaporation ponds, and two rock monitors _Varanus albigularis_ were rescued alive. Half of the casualties ( _n_ = 19), including all the mammals and reptiles, likely drowned as they were unable to escape from the ponds. The other mortalities were of waterbirds: one immature White-breasted Cormorant _Phalacrocorax lucidus_ and 17 chicks of birds breeding at the site (Table 1). Of four South African Shelduck _Tadorna cana_ chicks that were dissected, three showed evidence of internal trauma and haemorrhage, possibly due to attacks from Cape Teals _Anas capensis,_ which were observed to display aggressive behaviour towards other species. The other chicks were found in too advanced a state of decay to determine cause of death. Potential pollutant concentrations in water samples were all well within the South African Department of Water and Sanitation requirements, suggesting that selenium toxicity was unlikely to have caused any deaths (Herbst 2006).

## _**Searcher efficiency trials**_

Only 57% of small birds were detected compared with the 81% of medium and 100% of large birds (Table 2). Overall, searchers detected 72% of bird carcasses, with larger birds more likely to be detected than small birds (χ[2] = 28.15, df = 2, _p_ < 0.001).

## _**Carcass persistence trials**_

All large bird carcasses (>1 kg) remained detectable after 28 d, compared with 50% of medium-sized carcasses (100–1 000 g) and 22% of small carcasses (<100 g) (Figure 2, Supplementary Appendix S2). Of the carcasses deployed, 26% were scavenged during the trials and 6% were recorded as feather ‘spots’, but no carcasses were recorded as feather spots at the end of the 28-day trial (Supplementary Appendix S2). Species that scavenged at carcasses included Pied Crow _Corvus albus_ , Cape fox _Vulpes chama_ , slender mongoose _Galerella sanguinea_ and striped polecat _Ictonyx striatus_ (Supplementary Appendix S2).

## _**Fatality estimator**_

The total mortality ( _M_ ) estimate revealed, with 90% confidence, that no more than nine birds were killed in the facility over a full year. This relates to a maximum mortality rate of 0.2 bird fatalities MW[−1] y[−1] at the Bokpoort CSP facility. The mortality rate parameter (λ) revealed a mean of 3.9 (90% CI 0.0–14.9) mortalities y[−1] . Using the mortality rate parameter (λ), a mean of 0.1 bird fatalitites MW[−1] ·y[−1] (90% CI 0.0–0.3 birds) was calculated.

## _**Bird communities**_

A total of 81 bird species were recorded during the study. None is listed as threatened, but the Kori Bustard _Ardeotis kori_ is Near Threatened and 16 species are endemic or near-endemic to southern Africa (Taylor et al. 2015; Supplementary Appendix S3). Eight foraging guilds were represented, with granivores and insectivores the most abundant guilds (other guilds were frugivores, carnivores, nectarivores, omnivores, piscivores and aquatic; Supplementary Appendix S3).

Only 22 bird species were recorded in the solar field during 1 980 transects, covering 594 km at a mean (±SD) abundance of 0.38 ± 2.2 birds transect[−1] (1.3 birds km[−1] ). Of these, only six were recorded on more than five occasions: Familiar Chat _Cercomela familiaris_ , Cape Sparrow _Passer melanurus_ , Fawn-coloured Lark _Calendulauda africanoides_ , Sociable Weaver _Philetairus socius_ , Namaqua Dove _Oena capensis_ and Western Barn Owl. By comparison, 51 species were observed in 44 rangeland transects, with a crude abundance of 70.9 ± 37.8 birds transect[−1] (141.9 birds km[−1] ). The average density of 40 species seen within 50 m of the transect lines (Supplementary Appendix S4) was 55.0 ± 35.1 birds transect[−1] (110.0 birds km[−1] ). The 11 species not recorded within 50 m of the transect lines in rangeland included large species such as bustards, korhaans and raptors.

Despite less search effort than in the solar field, 34 rangeland species were absent from the solar field (Supplementary Appendix S3). Many of these species inhabit trees and shrubs, features not present in the solar field. Only three species were restricted to the solar field: House Sparrow _Passer domesticus_ , Mountain Wheatear _Oenanthe monticola_ and Western Barn Owl (Supplementary Appendix S3); all three benefit from the installation of infrastructure for foraging, roosting or breeding. Based on their primary food preference, most rangeland species were insectivores (55%) and granivores (27%) followed by carnivores (10%), frugivores (4%), omnivores (2%) and nectarivores (2%) (Supplementary Appendix S3). Most solar field birds also were insectivores (45%) or granivores (41%), with only one frugivore (5%), one omnivore (5%) and one carnivore (5%) (Supplementary Appendix S3). The solar field transects had significantly fewer bird species ( _Z_ = −16.94, _p_ < 0.001) and lower abundance ( _Z_ = −64.68, _p_ < 0.001) than adjacent rangelands.

At the evaporation ponds, 37 bird species were recorded during 53 counts (70.2 ± 16.5 per count) of which 23 species were only found at the ponds (Supplementary Appendix S3). Most (38%) species were assigned to the aquatic diet guild (aquatic invertebrates/plants), with 24% granivores, 24% insectivores, 11% piscivores and 3% frugivores (Supplementary Appendix S3).

## **Discussion**

## _**Bird and wildlife mortalities**_

The Bokpoort CSP Environmental Impact Assessment regarded collision impact and solar flux to be of moderate significance (van Rooyen 2010), but our results suggest that these impacts may be less significant than previously thought. Direct impacts as a result of collision trauma in the solar field were trivial compared with some other solar impact studies (e.g. Walston et al. 2016; Visser et al. 2019). The study period was relatively short, and may not have accounted for temporal variation in mortality rates, given

**Figure 2:** Detection probability of bird carcasses (small [<100 g], medium [100–1 000 g] and large [>1 000 g]) for a 28-day period, at 7-day intervals, used in the carcass persistence trials at the USSE Bokpoort CSP parabolic trough facility

the number of old carcasses found during the initial carcass sweep. However, collision impacts might be expected to peak when a facility is first constructed, and decrease thereafter, as the local fauna learns to adapt to the new infrastructure (Madsen and Boertmann 2008).

Solar flux trauma is considered a risk to birds at CSP parabolic trough systems, although no evidence has been reported yet (Walston et al. 2016). Accordingly, we did not find any bird carcasses showing evidence of solar flux trauma at the Bokpoort CSP facility. At CSP trough systems, the central receiver is an absorber tube positioned at the focal line and running the length of the parabolic mirror trough. The tube has high solar irradiance absorbance and low thermal remittance (Zhang et al. 2013) and the HTF inside the tube cannot exceed 400 °C (Cekirge and Elhassan 2015). At CSP towers, the receiver is situated at the top of the tower where temperatures regularly exceed 400 °C (Kagan et al. 2014). In addition, on extremely hot days, heliostats are reflected away from the receiver to focal stand-by points and creates pockets of hot air with temperatures high enough to burn passing birds (McCrary et al. 1986). The differences between the maximum temperatures and design could explain why solar flux trauma has only been documented at CSP tower systems.

In comparison to the low collision risk, the evaporation ponds were an unexpectedly high source of mortality (Table 1). Most industrial-scale solar power facilities are built in arid areas, where evaporation ponds are likely to attract animals from the surrounding landscape (Lovich and Ennen 2011). The evaporation ponds at Bokpoort have a slippery plastic lining, which inhibits escape, essentially having the same potential as reservoirs to drown animals (Anderson et al. 1999). Two broad mitigation strategies could reduce the risk of drownings, especially for terrestrial species. The first approach is to limit the number of animals visiting the ponds, e.g. by (1) improved fencing (USFWS 2016a); (2) covering the ponds with bird exclusion netting (Littauer et al. 1997; USFWS 2016b – although birds can become entrapped, creating an even greater impact; see Nemtzov and Olsvig-Whittaker 2003); or (3) installing alternative water-points outside of the facility. The second option is to make it possible for animals that fall in to escape the ponds by (1) deploying ‘ladders’ along the sides of the evaporation ponds (but there would need to be good coverage, and the ladders should not entangle animals); (2) integrating natural edges to evaporation ponds; (3) reducing the slope of the pond margins; or (4) developing a non-slip pond lining. The effectiveness of these strategies requires further analysis, testing and monitoring.

Searcher efficiency trials showed a bias towards detecting larger bird carcasses (Supplementary Appendix S1) as they are easier to spot and persist longer in the field (Ponce et al. 2010). Carcass persistence depends on many factors, such as habitat type, climate, predator and scavenger communities, carcass size, species and season (Smallwood 2007, 2013; Shaw et al. 2015; Urquhart et al. 2015; Costantini et al. 2016). Smaller carcasses were more likely to be removed by scavengers than larger carcasses, likely due to the physical difficulty for small predators, such as Pied Crows and slender mongooses, to remove large carcasses. Carcasses that disappeared tended to do so

shortly after deployment; after that they were damaged by invertebrate activity and UV radiation, presumably reducing desirability to scavengers. The collision mortality estimate for this facility revealed a mean of 3.9 birds (90% CI 0.0–14.9) killed per year or 0.1·bird fatalities MW y[−1] (90% CI 0.0–0.3). Visser et al. (2019) calculated an extrapolated mortality estimate for a 96 MW PV facility in the Northern Cape, South Africa as 435 (95% CI 133–805) birds y[−1] and 4.5 bird fatalities MW[−1] y[−1] (95% CI 1.5–8.5). Our fatality estimates were considerably lower, possibly indicating lower collision impact associated with CSP trough facilities. However, the low fatality estimates in our results could have been influenced by the short study period.

We could not conclude if the facility acted as an ecological trap for insectivores by attracting insects through polarised light emissions (Horvárth et al. 2010; Lovich and Ennen 2011; Kagan et al. 2014); however, there were fewer insectivorous birds in the facility than adjacent rangelands both in terms of species richness and abundance. We did not find any evidence of the ‘lake effect’ (Lovich and Ennen 2011) as no waterbirds were recorded away from the ponds within the solar facility. Therefore, apart from the unexpected impact of the evaporation ponds, habitat loss was perhaps the most significant impact of the facility for birds.

## _**Impact of habitat transformation**_

Like previous reports, we found that bird abundance and diversity is reduced in solar fields compared with adjacent land-use types (Kagan et al. 2014). The sparse vegetation cover in the solar field, coupled with increased human disturbance, presumably explains the low bird abundance. The facility supported three species that were not recorded in the adjacent rangeland, all of which benefited from the provision of structures on which to forage, roost or breed. The House Sparrow is an introduced species that is closely associated with human structures in southern Africa (Hockey et al. 2005). Mountain Wheatears prefer rocky habitats, and occur on nearby outcrops, but are absent from open plains. Most interesting was the large number of Western Barn Owls in the facility. They presumably moved into the area to take advantage of the abundance of suitable roost sites in the mirror support tubes. These tubes turn slowly during the day to keep the mirrors facing the sun, then revert to their start position in a few minutes at the end of the day. This regular movement presumably prevents owls breeding in the tubes. Providing breeding boxes along the perimeter fence might further increase the owl population.

CSP trough facilities have a larger footprint per MW than CSP tower facilities (Walston et al. 2016) and alter the habitat more than PV facilities (Visser et al. 2019). While a single facility may be relatively small from a landscape perspective, the cumulative effects of habitat loss and fragmentation from multiple facilities need to be considered. The South African Government’s target for solar energy of 9.4 GW (9 400 MW) by 2030 (DoE 2016b) extrapolates to 13 000–58 000 ha of land required for developments. If this land includes previously degraded agricultural or industrial areas instead of pristine natural habitats, the amount of habitat loss and associated negative impacts could be reduced. These cumulative effects need to be anticipated,

managed and monitored to avoid future negative impacts on bird communities. However, the Northern Cape has vast areas of largely untransformed rangeland, and almost all the species observed in the rangeland were common birds in the region. More pressing and widespread threats to rangeland species in the area result from overgrazing, erosion, invasive species and climate change (Atkinson 2007; Moncrieff et al. 2015; Guo et al. 2017).

## _**Conclusions and recommendations for management**_

Bird mortalities within the solar field were lower than reported at PV facilities in the same region (Visser et al. 2019) and at CSP towers in North America (Walston et al. 2016). We found little evidence of direct impact through collision trauma on birds. CSP tower heliostats are large flat mirrors that are widely spaced in largely untransformed habitat and thus pose a potentially significant collision risk for birds, especially in the early morning and evening when the mirrors are oriented vertically. By comparison, CSP trough facilities have parabolic mirrors in tight rows in a highly transformed landscape containing relatively few birds, greatly reducing the risk of collision impact.

The high mortality rate recorded at the evaporation ponds was unexpected and may be an overlooked impact associated with CSP facilities (and other artificial water bodies in arid areas). The impact could be mitigated by improving the perimeter fencing and/or providing secure drinking water to animals, but the most important intervention should be to not create slippery-sided ponds that trap mammals and reptiles. Such mitigation strategies will require monitoring to gauge their success.

The low mortality recorded within the solar field is encouraging. However, given the limited number of published accounts and the short duration of this study, we recommend that monitoring programmes to assess the impacts of USSE facilities on birds and other wildlife are implemented (e.g. as proposed by Huso et al. 2016; Jenkins et al. 2017).
